condition_overview.definition: PCOS is the most common endocrinopathy affecting women of childbearing age. It is characterised by a combination of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology, with complex downstream effects on reproductive, metabolic, dermatologic, and psychological health.

prevalence.general: 8% to 13% of women of childbearing age (American Family Physician 2023)
prevalence.range_by_criteria: 4% to 18% depending on diagnostic criteria used
prevalence.anovulatory_infertility: 90–95% of anovulatory women seeking infertility treatment have PCOS
prevalence.proportion_of_hyperandrogenism: 72% to 82% of causes of hyperandrogenism in women

pathophysiology.summary: PCOS pathophysiology is complex and multifactorial, involving genetic and environmental factors that contribute to deficient signalling in the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis and to ovarian and adrenal hyperandrogenism. Metabolic, dermatologic, and gynecologic features are thought to be subsequent manifestations of insulin resistance.

key_mechanisms.detail: Elevated LH (luteinising hormone) secretion relative to FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone), resulting in increased androgen production by theca cells and anovulatory cycles. LH/FSH ratio is altered in almost all patients with PCOS.

Ovarian and/or adrenal overproduction of androgens (testosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone/DHEA, androstenedione). High circulating testosterone and DHEA occur in 60–80% and 20–25% of women with PCOS respectively. Excess androgen changes female hormone regulation, causing menstrual irregularity and infertility.

Affects approximately 65–70% of women with PCOS, occurring independently of obesity. Hyperinsulinemia increases androgen production, reduces sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), raises free testosterone, and interferes with ovulation and fertility. May also promote endometrial cell proliferation.
Insulin resistance reduces hepatic production of SHBG, leading to increased free testosterone levels and amplified androgenic effects.
Most authors consider abnormal steroidogenesis of ovarian or adrenal origin to be the primary disorder in PCOS.

Polygenic inheritance. Approximately 20–40% of first-degree female relatives of women with PCOS develop PCOS themselves. Genes involved include those related to androgen biosynthesis (CYP17, CP21, CP11α, 17β-HSD5, SHBG), insulin action and secretion (INSR, IRS-1, IRS-2, CAPN10, PPARγ), gonadotropin secretion (follistatin), and pro-inflammatory genotypes (TNF-α, IL-6 variants).
Epigenetic and environmental factors such as unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and obesity can compound underlying genetic predisposition.

condition_overview.age_of_onset: Reproductive age; can manifest from adolescence
condition_overview.prognosis: PCOS is a lifelong condition but symptoms often improve with age. Androgen production tends to decrease near menopause, and menstrual cycles often become more regular. Long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risks persist beyond reproductive years.
condition_overview.importance_of_early_diagnosis: PCOS should be diagnosed and treated early in adolescence due to reproductive, metabolic, and oncological complications that may be associated with it.

diagnostic_criteria.overview: There is no single diagnostic test for PCOS. Clinical criteria are used. Three major diagnostic systems exist, with the Rotterdam Criteria (2003) being the most widely used.
diagnostic_criteria.gold_standard: None — PCOS is a clinical diagnosis based on exclusion of other conditions and meeting diagnostic criteria

criteria_systems.name: NIH Criteria
criteria: Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (with exclusion of other aetiologies)
criteria_systems.notes: Most restrictive criteria; requires both oligoanovulation AND hyperandrogenism. Does not include polycystic ovaries as a criterion.

criteria_systems.name: Rotterdam Criteria
criteria_systems.organisation: European Society for Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) / American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM)
criteria_systems.requirements: At least 2 of 3 criteria must be present (after exclusion of other conditions)
criteria: Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism
criteria_systems.polycystic_ovary_definition: At least one ovary with 12 or more follicles with diameters of 2–9 mm and/or increased ovarian volume >10 ml
criteria_systems.notes: Most widely used. Considered a compromise between NIH and AE-PCOS criteria. Upheld unanimously by the International PCOS Network in 2018. Prevalence estimated to be up to five times higher than when defined by NIH criteria.
criteria_systems.current_status: Current gold standard; endorsed by International PCOS Network 2018

criteria_systems.name: AE-PCOS Society Criteria
criteria: Clinical and/or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism
criteria_systems.notes: Considers PCOS as fundamentally an androgen excess disorder. Hyperandrogenism is mandatory.

oligoanovulation_definition.primary_amenorrhoea: By 15 years of age or more than 3 years after thelarche (breast development)
oligoanovulation_definition.1_to_3_years_postmenarche: Menses less often than every 21 days or more often than every 45 days
oligoanovulation_definition.3_years_postmenarche_to_menopause: Menses less often than every 21 days or more often than every 35 days, or fewer than 8 cycles per year
oligoanovulation_definition.1_year_postmenarche: A menstrual cycle lasting longer than 90 days
oligoanovulation_definition.note: If menses are regular but oligoanovulation is suspected, a serum progesterone level can be obtained about one week before anticipated menses

biochemical: Note: Measured at least 3 months after stopping hormonal contraception. Direct free testosterone assays should NOT be used.
clinical: Hirsutism — defined as modified Ferriman-Gallwey score ≥4 to 6 (depending on ethnicity); count only terminal hairs ≥5 mm in length and hyperpigmented
Androgenic alopecia (as defined by Ludwig visual scale)
Acne vulgaris (or severe acne vulgaris in adolescents)

polycystic_ovaries_on_ultrasound.definition: At least one ovary with ≥12 follicles with diameters 2–9 mm and/or increased ovarian volume >10 ml
polycystic_ovaries_on_ultrasound.caution: Ultrasound findings should NOT be used as a criterion within 8 years of menarche because of high incidence of multifollicular ovaries in this life stage
polycystic_ovaries_on_ultrasound.prevalence_in_normal_women: Found in as many as 62% of patients with normal ovulation; percentage declines with age

adolescent_diagnosis.special_criteria: Because Rotterdam criteria for adults overlap with normal pubertal physiologic changes, diagnosis in adolescents requires the presence of BOTH oligoanovulation AND hyperandrogenism for at least 2 years postmenarche.
adolescent_diagnosis.ultrasound_in_adolescents: NOT recommended as a diagnostic criterion because polycystic ovaries can be part of normal ovarian morphology in this age group. The International PCOS Network recommends waiting until at least 8 years after menarche to consider ultrasound findings.
adolescent_diagnosis.prevalence_of_polycystic_morphology_in_a: 30–40% of healthy adolescents have polycystic ovary morphology
adolescent_diagnosis.why_diagnosis_is_delayed: Oligoanovulation is common in the 2 years following menarche because of immaturity of the HPO axis. By the third year postmenarche, regular cycles (every 21–45 days) are established in 95% of adolescents.
adolescent_diagnosis.most_reliable_marker_in_teens: Progressive hirsutism is the most consistent marker for PCOS in the teenage years, as acne is common in adolescence and menstrual cycles often irregular for the first few years.
adolescent_diagnosis.recommended_deferral: A definitive diagnosis should be deferred until at least 2 years after onset of menstruation to assess whether other diagnostic criteria are met.
adolescent_diagnosis.treatment_before_diagnosis: Obesity-related hyperandrogenism and hyperinsulinemia can be treated before a PCOS diagnosis is confirmed.

exclusion_workup.minimum_evaluation: All nonpregnant patients with suspected PCOS should be evaluated to exclude thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinemia, and nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

differential_diagnosis_with_testing.clinical_clues: Change in hat/glove size, protruding jaw, impaired vision

differential_diagnosis_with_testing.testing: Calculated free testosterone level, free androgen index, or calculated bioavailable testosterone level (using high-quality measurement: liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry or extraction chromatography immunoassays); DHEA-S; ovarian ultrasound; adrenal CT or MRI
differential_diagnosis_with_testing.clinical_clues: Severe virilisation — change in voice, clitoromegaly, rapid onset

differential_diagnosis_with_testing.testing: Cortisol level (saliva or urine) or dexamethasone suppression test
differential_diagnosis_with_testing.clinical_clues: Dorsocervical fat pad, purple striae, hypertension

differential_diagnosis_with_testing.testing: HbA1c level, oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
FSH, LH, and oestradiol levels (ideally on day 3)
differential_diagnosis_with_testing.clinical_clues: Low body weight, eating disorder, or excessive exercise

clinical_features.overview: Patients with PCOS may be asymptomatic or may have multiple metabolic, dermatologic, or gynecologic manifestations. Presentation is highly variable — PCOS may manifest as a mild menstrual disorder or a severe disturbance of reproductive and metabolic functions.

gynecologic_features.prevalence: Nearly two-thirds of people with PCOS do not ovulate regularly
gynecologic_features.mechanism: Anovulation due to LH/FSH imbalance and hyperandrogenism

gynecologic_features.prevalence: PCOS is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility; 90–95% of anovulatory women seeking infertility treatment have PCOS
gynecologic_features.mechanism: Anovulation and follicular developmental arrest beyond 10 mm

gynecologic_features.prevalence_in_pcos: Approximately 75% of women with PCOS have polycysts on ovaries
gynecologic_features.note: Not necessary or sufficient for diagnosis alone

gynecologic_features.detail: Prolonged anovulation may lead to dysfunctional uterine bleeding that mimics menstrual bleeding. Women with oligo-ovulation may experience heavy bleeding when they do menstruate.
Women with PCOS who become pregnant are at higher risk of gestational diabetes mellitus and first-trimester spontaneous abortion

dermatologic_features.definition: Excessive growth of terminal hair in androgen-dependent areas of women (face, chest, abdomen, back, thighs)
dermatologic_features.prevalence_in_pcos: Approximately 70% of women with PCOS; present in 50–80% of patients with hyperandrogenism
dermatologic_features.prevalence_in_general_population: 10% of women of childbearing age without PCOS
dermatologic_features.assessment: Modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale; score >8 indicates hirsutism (or ≥4–6 depending on ethnicity in Rotterdam criteria)
dermatologic_features.mechanism: Increased 5α-reductase enzyme activity in hair follicles converts testosterone to DHT (dihydrotestosterone). Activity stimulated by hyperandrogenism, IGF-1, and insulin.
dermatologic_features.clinical_note: Self-treatment (waxing, shaving) is common and may limit clinical assessment. Count only terminal hairs ≥5 mm in length and hyperpigmented.

dermatologic_features.definition: Disorder of the pilosebaceous unit with lesions on face, neck, back, and chest
dermatologic_features.prevalence: Less common than hirsutism; may be present as a hirsutism equivalent for hyperandrogenism diagnosis
dermatologic_features.mechanism: Increased androgen sensitivity of sebaceous glands; local conversion of androgens. Association with DHEA-S, DHT, androstenedione, testosterone, and IGF-1.
dermatologic_features.note: Common in adolescence even without PCOS; acne alone is not a good marker for PCOS in teenagers

dermatologic_features.definition: Hair loss in the central region of the scalp (crown/part-line pattern in women)
dermatologic_features.mechanism: In presence of elevated androgens and higher 5α-reductase activity: shortened anagen phase, follicle miniaturisation, terminal hairs become vellus hairs
dermatologic_features.note: Most patients with androgenic alopecia have normal endocrine function; examine for other signs of hyperandrogenism

dermatologic_features.definition: Excess sebum production leading to oily skin
dermatologic_features.note: Less common than hirsutism and acne; may qualify as hirsutism equivalent

dermatologic_features.definition: Brown, velvety, raised skin patches in body folds — neck, armpits, groin, inframammary region, elbows
dermatologic_features.prevalence_in_pcos: Reported in approximately 5% of PCOS patients
dermatologic_features.clinical_significance: Indicates presence of significant insulin resistance; warrants glucose tolerance testing. When severe, extensive, and progressive — especially with mucosal involvement — may be associated with malignancy.
additional_signs: Rough, reddened hair follicles on upper arms

metabolic_features.prevalence: Affects approximately 65–70% of women with PCOS; occurs independently of obesity
metabolic_features.consequences: Compensatory hyperinsulinemia, increased androgen production, reduced SHBG, elevated free testosterone, impaired ovulation

metabolic_features.prevalence_igt: 30–40% of PCOS patients have impaired glucose tolerance (IGT)
metabolic_features.increased_risk: 2.5-fold increased prevalence of IGT; 4-fold increased prevalence of type 2 diabetes compared to women without PCOS
metabolic_features.annual_progression: Annual progression rate from normal glucose tolerance to IGT, and from IGT to type 2 diabetes, is substantially enhanced in women with PCOS, especially if obese with family history of T2DM

metabolic_features.detail: Patients with PCOS often have abnormal lipid levels
metabolic_features.lipid_pattern: Low HDL, elevated triglycerides, elevated LDL are common

metabolic_features.detail: PCOS is independently associated with a 37% greater risk of hypertension, even after adjusting for other comorbidities

metabolic_features.prevalence: 35–60% of women with PCOS are obese
metabolic_features.effect: Obesity worsens both metabolic and reproductive features of PCOS, particularly visceral adiposity
metabolic_features.note: Insulin resistance occurs independently of obesity in PCOS; women with PCOS may have metabolic abnormalities even at normal weight

metabolic_features.prevalence_us: 33–47% of women with PCOS in the United States have metabolic syndrome
metabolic_features.comparison: Two to three times higher rate than age-matched healthy women without PCOS
metabolic_features.link: Hyperinsulinemia may be a crucial link between PCOS and metabolic syndrome

metabolic_features.detail: Women with PCOS and metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes are at the highest risk of CVD. Women with PCOS have a 4- to 7-fold higher risk of heart attack than women of the same age without PCOS.

psychological_features.prevalence: More than twofold increased prevalence compared to women without PCOS
psychological_features.screening: Recommended for all patients with PCOS

psychological_features.prevalence: More than twofold increased prevalence compared to women without PCOS
psychological_features.screening: Recommended for all patients with PCOS

psychological_features.detail: Women with PCOS suffer from greater body dissatisfaction and are at increased risk of mood, generalised anxiety, and eating disorders
psychological_features.note: Physicians should minimise stigma and negative self-thoughts when discussing weight management

psychological_features.detail: PCOS affects quality of life across the lifespan through reproductive, metabolic, and psychological impacts

other_features.prevalence: Nearly fourfold increased prevalence compared to women without PCOS
other_features.screening: Recommended for all patients with PCOS

other_features.risk_increase: At least twofold increased risk compared to general population
other_features.mechanism: Chronic anovulation → prolonged oestrogen exposure without progesterone opposition → endometrial hyperplasia → cancer risk. Hyperinsulinemia promotes endometrial cell proliferation.
other_features.screening_recommendation: Routine endometrial cancer screening NOT recommended. Maintain low threshold for evaluation — transvaginal ultrasonography, endometrial biopsy, or both — for patients with prolonged amenorrhoea or abnormal uterine bleeding, especially if overweight.
other_features.prevention: Induce menses at least every 3–4 months to reduce risk of endometrial cancer

other_features.detail: Women with PCOS who have insulin resistance may experience hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia and report intense cravings for carbohydrates

diagnostic_workup.approach: A clinical diagnosis of PCOS can generally be made with a history, physical examination, and basic laboratory testing. No single diagnostic test exists.
history_points: Menstrual history — cycle length, regularity, duration
Symptoms of hyperandrogenism (hair growth, acne, scalp hair loss)
Family history — PCOS in first-degree female relatives, irregular periods, infertility in female relatives
Symptoms of insulin resistance — skin tags, acanthosis nigricans, carbohydrate cravings
physical_examination: Assessment for hirsutism using modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale
Skin examination — acne, seborrhoea, acanthosis nigricans, skin tags
Scalp hair assessment for androgenic alopecia
Signs of Cushing syndrome (dorsocervical fat pad, purple striae)

minimum_required.purpose: Mandatory to exclude pregnancy before any evaluation

androgen_testing.timing: At least 3 months after stopping hormonal contraception
androgen_testing.avoid: Direct free testosterone assays — not standardised
androgen_testing.limitation: Evaluation of androgen levels is complicated by lack of standardised testosterone assays in the United States

metabolic_testing.preferred: OGTT preferred in high-risk patients (BMI >25 kg/m² in non-Asian, >23 in Asian; history of impaired fasting glucose or gestational diabetes; family history of T2DM; hypertension; high-risk ethnicity)
metabolic_testing.pregnancy: All patients with PCOS should have a 75-g OGTT during preconception counselling. If not done preconception, offer OGTT at <20 weeks' gestation; if normal, repeat at 24–28 weeks.

metabolic_testing.timing: All patients with PCOS at baseline; repeat based on hyperlipidaemia and global CVD risk

metabolic_testing.frequency: Annually (or more often based on global CVD risk)

pelvic_ultrasound.diagnostic_criteria: ≥12 follicles 2–9 mm in diameter and/or ovarian volume >10 ml in at least one ovary
pelvic_ultrasound.limitation_in_adolescents: Not recommended as diagnostic criterion within 8 years of menarche due to high prevalence of multifollicular ovaries in adolescence
pelvic_ultrasound.clinical_use: Can diagnose polycystic ovary morphology. Also useful for monitoring response to ovulation induction treatment.

additional_screening.screening: Smoking status — counsel cessation if applicable
Cancer screening — follow universal recommendations; no additional PCOS-specific cancer screening recommended beyond endometrial evaluation when clinically indicated

pcos_phenotypes.overview: PCOS is a heterogeneous syndrome. The Rotterdam Criteria generate four possible phenotypes based on the combination of the three diagnostic features. Only a third of patients have the 'classic' form.

phenotypes.notes: Highest metabolic risk; classic presentation described by Stein and Leventhal in 1935
No polycystic ovary morphology on ultrasound
Regular ovulation present; women with chronic anovulation but normal androgen levels tend to not be insulin resistant
No clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism; lowest metabolic risk; only recognised by Rotterdam criteria, not NIH or AE-PCOS

overarching_principles: Treatment plans typically focus on specific symptoms as no single cure exists for the underlying pathophysiology.
Lifestyle modification is the foundation of therapy and a central component for all manifestations.
Subsequent management decisions depend on the patient's desire for pregnancy.
Physicians should explain the purpose of attempted weight loss with attention to minimising stigma and negative self-thoughts.
Smoking cessation is recommended for all patients with PCOS who smoke.

lifestyle_modification.recommendation: Multicomponent lifestyle intervention, including nutritional counselling, calorie-restricted diet, exercise, and behavioural strategies, is recommended for all patients with PCOS who are overweight.
lifestyle_modification.evidence: A 2019 Cochrane review concluded that lifestyle interventions may reduce free androgen index, body weight, and BMI, and increase SHBG levels. A 2018 systematic review found no significant differences among various diets for most outcomes but overall calorie-restricted diets benefited PCOS independently of weight loss.
lifestyle_modification.weight_loss_target: Weight loss exceeding 5% (some sources say 5–10%) of initial body weight has been linked to clinical improvement in fertility and metabolic parameters.
lifestyle_modification.even_without_weight_loss: Dietary intervention improves health and quality of life even in the absence of weight loss.
lifestyle_modification.no_superior_diet: No specific energy-equivalent diet appears to be superior; dietary changes should be tailored to food preferences. No specific dietary composition has been demonstrated to be most beneficial.
lifestyle_modification.low_glycaemic_diet: Subtle but inconclusive improvements were observed with a low-glycaemic diet; a nutritionally adequate weight loss diet based on healthy food choices is of clinical benefit regardless of composition.

benefits: Helps reduce chronic stress and stress-related eating

adolescents.aerobic: 60 minutes per day of moderate- to vigorous-intensity activity in bouts of ≥10 minutes

adults_18_to_64.moderate_intensity: 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity
adults_18_to_64.vigorous_intensity: 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity activity
adults_18_to_64.strength: At least 2 times per week on non-consecutive days

behaviour_strategies: Screening and treatment of mood and anxiety disorders

vitamin_d.detail: Vitamin D deficiency is common in women with PCOS. There is limited evidence that vitamin D supplementation may improve reproductive function and insulin sensitivity.
vitamin_d.recommendation: Vitamin D levels should be tested; supplementation may be warranted to increase low levels, especially in women undergoing IVF.
vitamin_d.note: More randomised controlled trials are needed

lifestyle_modification.delay_pharmacotherapy_for_weight_loss: A secondary analysis of two RCTs found that delaying ovulation-inducing pharmacotherapy until after achieving approximately 6% weight loss in a 16-week intervention resulted in a statistically significant increase in ovulation and live birth rates. ESHRE/ASRM recommend counselling on lifestyle modification before interventions for ovulation induction are considered.

medical_nutrition_therapy.framework: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics evidence-based nutrition practice guidelines
components: Thorough nutrition assessment to help prioritise MNT
Nutrition diagnosis (presence of, risk of, or potential for developing a nutritional deficit addressable by nutrition therapy)

Nutrition interventions (specific actions to remedy the nutrition diagnosis; clinical and behavioural goals agreed upon collaboratively; meal-planning strategy; education on portion sizes and healthy dining choices)
Nutrition monitoring and evaluation with ongoing follow-up to support long-term lifestyle changes, evaluate outcomes, and modify interventions as needed

pharmacological_management.overview: When lifestyle treatment does not result in desired outcomes, pharmacotherapy may be added. Treatment choice is guided by the patient's desire for pregnancy.

menstrual_irregularities.goal: Induce menses at least every 3–4 months to decrease the risk of endometrial cancer

first_line.evidence: Consistent evidence from RCTs showing improved outcomes (SORT Grade A)
first_line.detail: Lowest effective oestrogen dose such as 20–30 mcg ethinyl estradiol or its equivalent is preferred. Attention to contraindications and PCOS-specific risk factors (elevated BMI, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension).
first_line.avoid: Higher-dose (35 mcg) ethinyl estradiol preparations should NOT be first-line therapy due to increased risk of venous thromboembolism
first_line.preferred_progestins: Levonorgestrel, norethindrone, or norgestimate associated with lowest risk of thromboembolism
first_line.adolescents: 30 mcg ethinyl estradiol preparations may preserve peak bone mineral density. Preparations <30 mcg associated with lower bone mineral density in adolescents (fracture risk increase not observed).
first_line.long_acting_options: Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD or implant ideal for patients with difficulty adhering to oral contraceptives or contraindications to oestrogen. A 2020 Cochrane review found levonorgestrel-releasing IUD more effective than oral progesterone for reducing risk of endometrial hyperplasia progressing to endometrial cancer.
first_line.superior_to: Oral contraceptives are superior to metformin for menstrual regulation in adolescents and adults

options: Micronised progesterone 200 mg orally per day for 10–14 days
Medroxyprogesterone 5–10 mg orally per day for 5–10 days

second_line.dose: Daily dosage of 1,500 mg or higher
second_line.evidence: SORT Grade B — consistent evidence from RCTs showing improved outcomes, although likely inferior to lifestyle modification for diabetes prevention
second_line.benefits: Superior to placebo for management of weight, LDL cholesterol (BMI >25 kg/m²), and fasting glucose, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels regardless of BMI
second_line.dose_ceiling: An 8-month RCT showed 2,500 mg daily has minimal additional benefit over 1,500 mg

second_line.caution: MUST be prescribed with effective contraception — antiandrogens can cause undervirilisation in a male fetus
second_line.timing: Consider adding antiandrogens only if at least 6 months of oral contraceptive use AND cosmetic therapies alone do not sufficiently improve symptoms
second_line.when_oc_contraindicated: When oral contraceptives are contraindicated or poorly tolerated, use another form of effective contraception with antiandrogens

hirsutism.third_line: Metformin (may be less effective than oral contraceptives, particularly in those with BMI 25–30 kg/m²)

acne.first_line: Hormonal contraception with or without standard topical acne therapy
acne.second_line: Antiandrogen medications (e.g., spironolactone) — must be used with contraception

androgenic_alopecia.second_line: Antiandrogen medications — must be used with contraception

overweight_obesity.second_line: Anti-obesity medications (when lifestyle modification is insufficient)

second_line.indication_adults: For adult PCOS patients with IGT or T2DM when lifestyle interventions alone are not sufficient
second_line.indication_adolescents: For adolescent patients with IGT or metabolic syndrome
second_line.mechanism: Improves insulin sensitivity, decreases circulating androgen levels, normalises menstrual cycle and ovulation

seeking_pregnancy.overview: Management for women seeking pregnancy focuses on ovulation induction, insulin sensitisation, and addressing infertility.
seeking_pregnancy.preconception_counselling: ESHRE/ASRM recommend lifestyle modification including modest weight loss and physical activity before interventions for ovulation induction are considered. Smoking cessation and reducing alcohol consumption should be emphasised.

first_line.dose: 2.5 mg orally per day for 5 days; typically start on day 3 of menstrual cycle (day 2–5 acceptable)
first_line.titration: If pregnancy not achieved, repeat same dose; if still unsuccessful, increase to 5 mg daily
first_line.regulatory_status: Used off-label for PCOS (clomiphene is FDA-approved; letrozole is not for this indication)
first_line.evidence: SORT Grade A — consistent evidence from RCTs showing improved outcomes for ovulation rate, pregnancy rate, and live birth rate. A 2018 systematic review concluded letrozole is superior to clomiphene for ovulation rate per patient, pregnancy rate, and live birth rate per patient.
first_line.live_birth_advantage: Meta-analysis showed letrozole has higher live birth rate vs clomiphene; number needed to treat = 10 for one additional live birth
first_line.multiple_pregnancy_rate: 3.4% with letrozole vs 7.4% with clomiphene (difference not statistically significant)

second_line.dose: 50 mg orally per day for 5 days; typically start on day 3 of menstrual cycle
second_line.regulatory_status: FDA-approved for treatment of ovulatory dysfunction
second_line.note: Preferred over metformin alone; however, combining clomiphene and metformin has shown higher pregnancy and live birth rates in patients with BMI >30 kg/m²
second_line.induction_of_menses: Progesterone induction required if no spontaneous menses: micronised progesterone 200 mg/day for 10–14 days OR medroxyprogesterone 5–10 mg/day for 5–10 days

third_line.role: Adjunctive therapy; third-line for ovulation induction alone
third_line.combination_advantage: Combining with clomiphene shows higher pregnancy and live birth rates when BMI >30 kg/m²

anovulation_infertility.counselling: Patients should be counselled about the elevated risk of multiple pregnancy with ovulation induction drugs

hirsutism_when_seeking_pregnancy.note: Hormonal treatments and antiandrogens are not safe in pregnancy

acne_when_seeking_pregnancy.first_line: Standard topical acne therapy (retinoids, antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide)

typical_dose.letrozole: 2.5 mg/day for 5 days (start day 2–5 of cycle); max 7.5 mg/day
typical_dose.clomiphene: 50 mg/day for 5 days (start day 2–5 of cycle); max 100 mg/day, up to 6 cycles

approximate_monthly_cost.clomiphene: $6 (generic; brand no longer available) for five 50-mg tablets

letrozole_vs_clomiphene.multiple_pregnancy_risk: No statistical difference between letrozole and clomiphene
letrozole_vs_clomiphene.miscarriage_risk: No statistical difference between letrozole and clomiphene
letrozole_vs_clomiphene.regulatory_note: Clomiphene is FDA-approved; letrozole is used off-label for PCOS

comorbidity_management.title: Management of Comorbidities in PCOS
comorbidity_management.summary: Patients with PCOS should be evaluated for and managed for dyslipidaemia, hypertension, dysglycaemia, smoking, obstructive sleep apnoea, and depression. Additional cancer screening beyond standard recommendations is NOT required.

comorbidities.screening: Assess glycaemic status at baseline using OGTT, fasting plasma glucose, or HbA1c; repeat every 1–3 years
high_risk_criteria: BMI >25 kg/m² in non-Asian; >23 kg/m² in Asian patients
History of impaired fasting glucose or gestational diabetes
comorbidities.pregnancy: All PCOS patients should have a 75-g OGTT during preconception counselling

comorbidities.screening: Obtain fasting lipid profile in all patients with PCOS; repeat based on hyperlipidaemia and global CVD risk
Blood pressure measurement annually (or more often based on global CVD risk)

comorbidities.intervention: Counsel patient about smoking cessation if applicable

comorbidities.screening: Screen for depression in all PCOS patients
Screen for sleep apnoea in all PCOS patients
comorbidities.prevalence: Nearly fourfold increased prevalence vs women without PCOS

comorbidities.risk: At least twofold increased risk; absolute risk is relatively low
comorbidities.screening: No routine endometrial cancer screening recommended. Maintain low threshold for evaluation in patients with prolonged amenorrhoea or abnormal uterine bleeding (especially overweight): use transvaginal ultrasonography, endometrial biopsy, or both.
comorbidities.prevention: Induce menses at least every 3–4 months in patients with oligomenorrhoea

pcos_and_fertility.overview: PCOS is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility and the main source of female infertility in many countries. Infertility is related to hypersecretion of LH (70% of anovulatory women with PCOS), elevated LH/FSH ratio, and increased ovarian androgen production resulting in anovulatory cycles.
pcos_and_fertility.mechanism_of_infertility: PCOS is characterised by anovulation due to a developmental defect of follicles beyond 10 mm in size. Most cycles are anovulatory, making ovulation induction essential.

fertility_statistics.pcos_in_anovulatory_infertility: 90–95% of anovulatory women seeking infertility treatment have PCOS
fertility_statistics.pcos_in_amenorrhea_patients: 30–40% of patients with primary or secondary amenorrhoea have PCOS
fertility_statistics.pcos_in_oligomenorrhea_patients: 80% of patients with oligomenorrhoea have PCOS

obesity_and_fertility.detail: Approximately 50% of infertile women also have obesity. chatbot_faq.question: What is PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common hormonal disorder affecting women of childbearing age, estimated to affect 8–13% of women globally. It involves a combination of problems including irregular or absent periods, signs of excess male hormones (androgens) such as excess hair growth and acne, and sometimes small cysts on the ovaries. It also has important metabolic effects including insulin resistance, increased risk of type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The exact cause is not fully understood but involves a mix of genetic and environmental factors.

chatbot_faq.question: How common is PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS affects 8–13% of women of childbearing age (some sources report 4–18% depending on diagnostic criteria used). Approximately 105 million women aged 15–49 worldwide are estimated to have PCOS. It is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility, accounting for 90–95% of anovulatory women seeking infertility treatment.

chatbot_faq.question: What are the symptoms of PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS symptoms vary widely and can include: (1) Reproductive/gynecological: irregular or absent periods, difficulty getting pregnant, heavy bleeding when periods do occur; (2) Dermatological: excess hair growth (hirsutism) on face, chest, abdomen or back, acne, oily skin, scalp hair thinning or loss (androgenic alopecia), dark velvety skin patches (acanthosis nigricans); (3) Metabolic: weight gain, difficulty losing weight, intense carbohydrate cravings, signs of insulin resistance; (4) Psychological: depression, anxiety, body dissatisfaction. Some women with PCOS have no symptoms at all.

chatbot_faq.question: Can PCOS cause weight gain?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Between 35–60% of women with PCOS are overweight or obese. Insulin resistance — which affects 65–70% of women with PCOS — contributes to weight gain and makes it harder to lose weight. However, PCOS can also occur in women of normal weight. Even without obesity, insulin resistance in PCOS can cause metabolic problems.

chatbot_faq.question: What is hirsutism and how does it relate to PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Hirsutism is the excessive growth of terminal (coarse, dark) hair in androgen-dependent areas of women's bodies — such as the face (upper lip, chin), chest, abdomen, and back. It occurs in approximately 70% of women with PCOS and is considered one of the best clinical markers of excess androgen (hyperandrogenism). It is assessed using the modified Ferriman-Gallwey scale; a score greater than 8 indicates significant hirsutism (some criteria use ≥4–6 depending on ethnicity). Self-treatment such as waxing or shaving is common and may reduce the apparent severity on assessment.

chatbot_faq.question: Can PCOS cause hair loss on the scalp?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Androgenic alopecia (pattern hair loss) can occur in women with PCOS due to excess androgens. It typically presents as diffuse thinning over the crown of the scalp (central part-line widening) rather than the hairline recession seen in men. It is assessed using the Ludwig visual scale. This can have significant psychosocial impact. Most patients with androgenic alopecia actually have normal endocrine function, so other signs of hyperandrogenism should be assessed alongside.

chatbot_faq.question: What is acanthosis nigricans and is it related to PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Acanthosis nigricans is a skin condition characterised by brown, velvety, raised patches in skin folds — most commonly on the neck, armpits, groin, and under the breasts. It occurs in approximately 5% of women with PCOS and is a sign of significant insulin resistance. Skin tags and rough patches on the elbows may also appear. When severe and extensive, especially with mucosal involvement, it may indicate an underlying malignancy, though this is uncommon.

chatbot_faq.question: How is PCOS diagnosed?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS is diagnosed clinically using the Rotterdam Criteria (2003), the most widely accepted diagnostic system. After excluding other conditions, a diagnosis requires at least 2 of 3 features: (1) Oligoanovulation (irregular or absent ovulation/periods), (2) Hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical signs of excess androgens), (3) Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. There is no single blood test for PCOS. A pregnancy test, TSH, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are checked first to exclude other conditions.

chatbot_faq.question: Is a blood test enough to diagnose PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: No single blood test can diagnose PCOS. Blood tests are used to support the diagnosis and exclude other conditions. Hormonal tests (free testosterone, free androgen index) help confirm hyperandrogenism. Blood tests for TSH, prolactin, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are done to rule out thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Metabolic tests (glucose, lipids) assess comorbidities. The diagnosis ultimately requires clinical assessment using the Rotterdam Criteria.

chatbot_faq.question: Do I need an ultrasound to be diagnosed with PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Not necessarily. An ultrasound showing polycystic ovaries is just one of three Rotterdam criteria. If you already meet 2 of the 3 criteria (e.g., irregular periods AND clinical signs of hyperandrogenism), an ultrasound is not required to make the diagnosis. If you only have one of the other two criteria, an ultrasound finding of polycystic ovaries could complete the diagnosis. Importantly, polycystic ovaries are found on ultrasound in up to 62% of women with normal ovulation — so the ultrasound alone is not diagnostic.

chatbot_faq.question: Can teenagers be diagnosed with PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes, but diagnosis in adolescents is more challenging because irregular periods and polycystic ovaries can be a normal part of puberty. In adolescents, both oligoanovulation AND hyperandrogenism must be present for at least 2 years after the first period (menarche) to diagnose PCOS. Ultrasound findings are NOT used as a diagnostic criterion in this age group because polycystic ovary morphology is present in 30–40% of healthy adolescents. Progressive hirsutism is the most reliable early marker in teenagers.

chatbot_faq.question: Can PCOS be diagnosed if I have regular periods?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes, potentially. The Rotterdam Criteria only require 2 of 3 features. If you have regular periods (ruling out oligoanovulation as a criterion), you could still be diagnosed with PCOS if you have BOTH hyperandrogenism AND polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. This is sometimes called 'ovulatory PCOS' or PCOS phenotype C.

chatbot_faq.question: Does having cysts on my ovaries mean I have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Not necessarily. Polycystic ovaries — follicles of 2–9 mm in diameter on ultrasound — are found in up to 62% of women with completely normal ovulation. These are normal follicles at various stages of development, not the large fluid-filled cysts associated with conditions like ovarian cyst disease. Polycystic ovary morphology alone does not confirm PCOS; you need to meet at least 2 of the 3 Rotterdam Criteria.

chatbot_faq.question: Is PCOS curable?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS is a chronic condition — there is no cure. However, it is very manageable. Symptoms can be significantly reduced with lifestyle changes and medications. The underlying hormonal imbalance persists but may improve over time, particularly as women approach menopause when androgen production naturally decreases. Many women with PCOS go on to have regular periods, successful pregnancies, and a good quality of life with appropriate management.

chatbot_faq.question: What is the first step in treating PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: The first-line treatment for all women with PCOS (especially those who are overweight) is lifestyle modification — this includes a calorie-restricted diet, regular physical activity, and behavioural strategies. Even a modest weight loss of 5–10% of body weight can significantly improve periods, fertility, hormonal levels, and metabolic health. Dietary changes improve health even without weight loss. After lifestyle interventions, the choice of further treatment depends on what symptoms are most troublesome and whether you want to become pregnant.

chatbot_faq.question: What diet should I follow if I have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: No single diet has been proven superior for PCOS. The key principles are: (1) Reduce total calories if overweight; (2) Eat regular balanced meals with carbohydrates, protein, and healthy fats at each meal to stabilise blood sugar; (3) A low-glycaemic diet (focusing on whole grains, legumes, vegetables, lean protein) shows some benefits; (4) Increase omega-3 fatty acids (nuts, flaxseeds, chia seeds, oily fish); (5) Avoid skipping meals, especially breakfast; (6) Distribute carbohydrates throughout the day rather than consuming mostly at night. Tailor dietary changes to your food preferences and cultural background for long-term sustainability.

chatbot_faq.question: How much exercise should I do with PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: For adults aged 18–64: aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity activity (such as brisk walking) OR 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity activity (such as running), plus strength training at least 2 times per week on non-consecutive days. For adolescents: 60 minutes per day of moderate- to vigorous-intensity activity, plus strength training at least 3 times per week. Exercise improves insulin sensitivity, reduces androgens, helps with weight management, improves lipid levels, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood.

chatbot_faq.question: What medications are used to treat PCOS if I don't want to get pregnant?
chatbot_faq.answer: If you do not want to become pregnant, the main treatments are: (1) Hormonal contraception (oral contraceptive pills) — first-line for irregular periods, hirsutism, and acne; (2) Antiandrogen medications such as spironolactone — second-line for hirsutism and acne (must always be used with contraception as they can harm a male fetus); (3) Metformin — used for insulin resistance, metabolic abnormalities, and as second-line for irregular periods; (4) Anti-obesity medications — if overweight and lifestyle changes insufficient. Lifestyle modification remains the foundation alongside all these treatments.

chatbot_faq.question: Do I need to take the contraceptive pill for PCOS even if I don't need contraception?
chatbot_faq.answer: If you have PCOS and irregular or absent periods but don't need contraception, the pill is still often recommended because it protects the lining of the womb (endometrium) from the effects of unopposed oestrogen, which can lead to endometrial hyperplasia and increase the risk of endometrial cancer. You must have a period (or a withdrawal bleed) at least every 3–4 months. If you don't want the pill, an alternative is periodic progesterone withdrawal — taking progesterone tablets for 10–14 days every few months to trigger a withdrawal bleed.

chatbot_faq.question: What is spironolactone and how does it help PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Spironolactone is an antiandrogen medication that blocks the effects of male hormones (androgens) in the body. In PCOS, it is used as a second-line treatment for hirsutism (excess hair growth) and acne when hormonal contraception alone has not been effective after at least 6 months of use. It is highly effective at reducing facial and body hair and improving acne. IMPORTANT: Spironolactone MUST always be used with effective contraception because it can cause undervirilisation (abnormal development) in a male fetus.

chatbot_faq.question: Can metformin help PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Metformin (typically at a daily dose of 1,500 mg or higher) helps treat PCOS by improving insulin sensitivity. This reduces circulating androgen levels, can help normalise menstrual cycles and ovulation, and helps manage blood sugar, cholesterol, and triglyceride levels. It is the first-line drug treatment for metabolic manifestations of PCOS (insulin resistance, dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia), and a second-line option for menstrual irregularities. However, it is likely inferior to lifestyle modification — particularly for preventing diabetes.

chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS cause infertility?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility — infertility caused by not releasing eggs (anovulation). However, having PCOS does not mean you cannot get pregnant. Most women with PCOS can conceive, often with treatment. With lifestyle changes, ovulation induction medications (like letrozole or clomiphene), or assisted reproductive technologies (IVF), the majority of women with PCOS who want to conceive are able to do so.

chatbot_faq.question: What is the best treatment if I have PCOS and want to get pregnant?
chatbot_faq.answer: The first step is lifestyle modification — even a 5–10% weight loss can restore spontaneous ovulation in some women. If that is not enough, the first-line medical treatment for ovulation induction is letrozole (2.5 mg/day for 5 days per cycle). Letrozole is superior to the older drug clomiphene for live birth rates. Clomiphene is the second-line option. Metformin may be added (especially if BMI >30 kg/m²). If oral treatments fail, assisted reproductive technologies (ART) including IVF may be offered.

chatbot_faq.question: What is letrozole and how does it help with PCOS fertility?
chatbot_faq.answer: Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor — a medication that temporarily lowers oestrogen levels, which stimulates the brain to release more FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone), triggering the ovaries to develop and release an egg. It is taken as a 2.5 mg tablet once daily for 5 days per cycle, starting on day 2–5 of the menstrual cycle. If no pregnancy after one cycle, the dose can be increased up to 7.5 mg. It is now the first-line fertility treatment for PCOS, and studies show it produces higher live birth rates than clomiphene. It is used off-label (not FDA-approved for PCOS, but this is well-supported by evidence).

chatbot_faq.question: What is clomiphene and how is it different from letrozole?
chatbot_faq.answer: Clomiphene (also called clomid) is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator. It blocks oestrogen receptors in the brain, tricking the body into producing more FSH to stimulate egg development. It has been used for decades and is FDA-approved for ovulatory dysfunction. However, research now shows letrozole has higher live birth rates and fewer multiple pregnancies. Clomiphene is therefore second-line after letrozole. Both drugs carry a small increased risk of twins or multiple pregnancies.

chatbot_faq.question: Should I lose weight before trying to get pregnant with PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes, weight loss before fertility treatment is generally recommended. A secondary analysis of two RCTs found that delaying ovulation-inducing pharmacotherapy until after achieving approximately 6% weight loss in a 16-week programme resulted in significantly higher rates of ovulation and live birth. Both ESHRE and ASRM (the major reproductive medicine societies) recommend lifestyle modification including modest weight loss before interventions for ovulation induction are considered. Even a 5–10% reduction in body weight can significantly improve fertility in overweight women with PCOS.

chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS increase my risk of diabetes?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes, significantly. Women with PCOS have a 2.5-fold increased prevalence of impaired glucose tolerance (pre-diabetes) and a 4-fold increased prevalence of type 2 diabetes compared to women without PCOS. Approximately 30–40% of PCOS patients have impaired glucose tolerance and 7.5–10% have type 2 diabetes. The annual progression from normal glucose to impaired glucose, and from impaired glucose to type 2 diabetes, is substantially faster in women with PCOS — especially if obese with a family history of diabetes.

chatbot_faq.question: How should I be screened for diabetes if I have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Your doctor should assess your blood sugar levels at baseline using an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), fasting plasma glucose, or HbA1c. The OGTT (75g glucose drink, measured at 2 hours) is preferred for high-risk patients (BMI >25 kg/m² in non-Asian women, >23 kg/m² in Asian women; history of impaired fasting glucose or gestational diabetes; family history of T2DM; hypertension; or high-risk ethnicity). chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS increase my risk of heart disease?

In the US, 33–47% of women with PCOS have metabolic syndrome, 2–3 times the rate of age-matched healthy women. Women with PCOS who also have metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes are at the highest CVD risk. Regular monitoring of blood pressure and lipids is essential.

chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS increase the risk of cancer?
chatbot_faq.answer: Women with PCOS have at least a twofold increased risk of endometrial (womb lining) cancer compared to the general population. This is because chronic anovulation leads to prolonged oestrogen exposure without progesterone, which can cause endometrial hyperplasia (thickening) that may progress to cancer. Obesity also contributes. However, the absolute risk remains relatively low. Routine endometrial cancer screening is not recommended, but a low threshold for evaluation should be maintained — particularly if you have prolonged absent periods or abnormal bleeding.

chatbot_faq.question: Can PCOS affect my mental health?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Women with PCOS have more than twice the prevalence of depression and anxiety compared to women without PCOS. They also suffer from greater body dissatisfaction and are at increased risk of eating disorders. The physical symptoms of PCOS (hirsutism, acne, weight gain, hair loss) can significantly affect self-image and psychological wellbeing. All women with PCOS should be screened for depression and anxiety and offered evidence-based treatment when needed. Regular physical activity can also help improve mood and body image.

chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS cause sleep problems?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Women with PCOS have a nearly fourfold increased prevalence of obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) compared to women without PCOS. OSA causes breathing interruptions during sleep, leading to poor sleep quality, daytime fatigue, and increased cardiovascular risk. All women with PCOS should be screened for sleep apnoea. If you experience loud snoring, waking up gasping, or excessive daytime sleepiness, discuss this with your doctor.

chatbot_faq.question: Is PCOS genetic — will I pass it on?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS has a significant genetic component. Approximately 20–40% of first-degree female relatives of women with PCOS will develop PCOS themselves (compared to 4–6% prevalence in the general population). Many women with PCOS have female relatives with the condition, even if it was never formally diagnosed (e.g., mothers or sisters with irregular periods or infertility). The genetic inheritance is polygenic — many genes each make a small contribution — compounded by environmental and lifestyle factors.

chatbot_faq.question: What causes PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: The exact cause of PCOS is not fully known. It is understood to be a complex multifactorial condition with both genetic and environmental contributions. Key factors include: (1) Genetic predisposition (polygenic — many genes involved in androgen synthesis, insulin signalling, and inflammation); (2) Insulin resistance — possibly from genetic variants in insulin receptors and related enzymes; (3) Dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis — leading to elevated LH and abnormal androgen production; (4) Abnormal steroidogenesis — excessive androgen production by the ovaries and/or adrenal glands; (5) Environmental triggers — unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and obesity can amplify underlying genetic predisposition.

chatbot_faq.question: My teenage daughter has irregular periods. Could she have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Irregular periods are common in the first 2–3 years after a girl's first period (menarche) because the hormonal axis is still maturing. By the third year after menarche, 95% of adolescents have established regular cycles (every 21–45 days). If irregular periods persist beyond 2 years after menarche and your daughter also has clinical signs of excess androgens (progressive hirsutism — not just common adolescent acne), PCOS should be considered. An ultrasound is NOT used to diagnose PCOS in adolescents. A formal PCOS evaluation including blood tests for hormones (testosterone, TSH, prolactin, 17-OHP) is recommended.

chatbot_faq.question: Can I have a healthy pregnancy if I have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes — most women with PCOS can have healthy pregnancies, though they face higher risks than women without PCOS. Women with PCOS who become pregnant have an increased risk of gestational diabetes mellitus and first-trimester miscarriage. They should be monitored closely during pregnancy. A 75-g OGTT should be offered at <20 weeks' gestation (if not done preconception), and repeated at 24–28 weeks if normal. Good glycaemic control, weight management, and regular antenatal care are important.

chatbot_faq.question: What screening should I have before trying to conceive if I have PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Before trying to conceive with PCOS, you should have: (1) A 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) to check for diabetes or pre-diabetes; (2) A fasting lipid profile; (3) Blood pressure check; (4) Screening for depression and obstructive sleep apnoea; (5) Discussion about lifestyle changes (weight loss, diet, exercise) before starting fertility treatments — this significantly improves outcomes. Your doctor may also check for other infertility causes (partner's sperm, tubal patency) before starting ovulation induction.

chatbot_faq.question: Could my PCOS be missed or misdiagnosed?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes — PCOS is frequently underdiagnosed. This happens because: (1) PCOS has many different presentations (phenotypes), so one woman's experience can be very different from another's; (2) Symptoms like irregular periods and acne are common and often dismissed; (3) Oral contraceptive use can 'hide' PCOS by regulating periods and lowering androgen levels; (4) Androgen testing can be unreliable if done while on hormonal contraception; (5) Not all clinicians are familiar with the full diversity of PCOS presentations. If you suspect you have PCOS, ask your GP or gynaecologist for a full PCOS evaluation.

chatbot_faq.question: Can the contraceptive pill hide PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Yes. Oral contraceptives can temporarily mask PCOS by lowering androgen levels, preventing visible signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne), and regulating the menstrual cycle. Women may only discover they have PCOS when they stop the pill (e.g., when trying to conceive) and symptoms reappear. For accurate androgen testing, blood tests should be done at least 3 months after stopping hormonal contraception.

chatbot_faq.question: Should I take vitamin D for PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Vitamin D deficiency is common in women with PCOS. There is some evidence that vitamin D supplementation may improve reproductive function and insulin sensitivity. Testing vitamin D levels is recommended, and supplementation may be warranted if levels are low — particularly in women undergoing IVF. However, more randomised controlled trials are needed before a strong recommendation can be made. Discuss with your doctor or dietitian whether supplementation is appropriate for you.

chatbot_faq.question: How is PCOS-related acne treated?
chatbot_faq.answer: Acne in PCOS is best treated by addressing the underlying hormonal imbalance: (1) Hormonal contraception (oral contraceptive pill) is first-line — it reduces androgen levels that drive acne; (2) Standard topical acne therapy (retinoids, antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide) can be combined with the pill or used alongside; (3) If acne persists after at least 6 months of oral contraceptive use, antiandrogen medications such as spironolactone can be added (second-line) — must always be used with contraception; (4) Metformin is third-line for acne in PCOS.

chatbot_faq.question: Does stress make PCOS worse?
chatbot_faq.answer: Chronic stress can worsen PCOS indirectly. Stress triggers the release of cortisol and other hormones that can increase insulin resistance, promote weight gain (particularly abdominal fat), and worsen inflammation — all of which aggravate PCOS symptoms. Stress can also trigger stress-related eating and poor dietary choices. Women with PCOS should be screened for mood and anxiety disorders, and stress-management strategies (regular exercise, mindfulness, adequate sleep) should be part of comprehensive PCOS management.

chatbot_faq.question: Can I reverse PCOS with diet and exercise alone?
chatbot_faq.answer: While PCOS cannot be 'reversed' (it is a lifelong condition), diet and exercise can dramatically improve or even resolve many symptoms. For overweight women with PCOS, losing even 5–10% of body weight through diet and exercise has been shown to restore menstrual regularity, improve or restore ovulation, reduce androgen levels, improve insulin sensitivity, and enhance quality of life — sometimes without any medication. For some women, lifestyle changes alone are sufficient. Dietary changes improve health even without significant weight loss.

chatbot_faq.question: What is the difference between the NIH, Rotterdam, and AE-PCOS diagnostic criteria?
chatbot_faq.answer: The three main diagnostic systems for PCOS differ in how strict they are: (1) NIH Criteria (1990) — the most restrictive; requires BOTH chronic anovulation AND clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism. This is the current recommended standard. (3) AE-PCOS Society Criteria (2006) — requires hyperandrogenism as mandatory plus ovarian dysfunction (anovulation and/or polycystic ovaries). The Rotterdam criteria identify the broadest group of patients.

chatbot_faq.question: Does PCOS get better with age?
chatbot_faq.answer: For many women, PCOS symptoms tend to improve over time. As women approach menopause, androgen production naturally decreases, menstrual cycles often become more regular, and reproductive symptoms improve. However, the underlying metabolic risks (insulin resistance, cardiovascular disease risk) may persist or even worsen if not actively managed throughout life. Research on the impact of PCOS on cardiovascular risk in postmenopausal years is still inconclusive. Lifelong monitoring of blood pressure, lipids, and blood sugar remains important.

chatbot_faq.question: What are anti-obesity medications and when are they used in PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Anti-obesity medications are used as second-line treatment for overweight or obese women with PCOS when lifestyle modification alone has not been sufficient. They are not a replacement for diet and exercise but can support greater weight loss and metabolic improvement. Examples include GLP-1 receptor agonists (such as semaglutide or liraglutide), which also have evidence for improving insulin resistance — particularly relevant in PCOS. Your doctor will discuss the most appropriate option based on your health profile.

chatbot_faq.question: Is PCOS related to polycystic kidney disease?
chatbot_faq.answer: No. PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) and polycystic kidney disease (PKD) are completely different and unrelated conditions. PCOS involves small follicular cysts on the ovaries as part of a hormonal syndrome, whereas PKD involves large fluid-filled cysts in the kidneys caused by a genetic mutation. Having PCOS does not increase your risk of PKD.

chatbot_faq.question: Can men be affected by PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: PCOS is a condition that specifically affects people with ovaries. However, male relatives of women with PCOS may carry related genetic variants that manifest differently — for example, insulin resistance, early-onset baldness, or metabolic syndrome. First-degree male relatives (brothers, sons) of women with PCOS may have higher rates of metabolic and hormonal abnormalities, though they do not develop PCOS itself.

chatbot_faq.question: When should I see a specialist for PCOS?
chatbot_faq.answer: Most PCOS can be managed by a GP (general practitioner) or family physician. You should consider a specialist referral (gynaecologist, endocrinologist, reproductive endocrinologist, or fertility specialist) if: (1) You are having difficulty conceiving and need ovulation induction; (2) Your symptoms are severe or not responding to standard treatment; (3) You have significant metabolic complications (uncontrolled diabetes, severe metabolic syndrome); (4) The diagnosis is uncertain; (5) You need advanced fertility treatments such as IVF; (6) You have significant psychological complications needing specialist support.

chatbot_faq.question: What is the connection between PCOS and insulin resistance?
chatbot_faq.answer: Insulin resistance is central to PCOS pathophysiology and is present in approximately 65–70% of women with PCOS — even those of normal weight. When cells don't respond properly to insulin, the pancreas compensates by producing more insulin (hyperinsulinemia). This excess insulin then: (1) Stimulates the ovaries and adrenal glands to produce more androgens; (2) Reduces the liver's production of SHBG, raising free testosterone levels; (3) Interferes with follicle development and ovulation; (4) Promotes endometrial cell proliferation. This is why treating insulin resistance (through lifestyle modification, metformin, or newer agents) is fundamental to managing PCOS.

patient_education_leaflet.title: Understanding PCOS — A Guide for Patients

sections.heading: What is PCOS?
sections.content: PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) is a hormonal condition affecting 1 in 10 women of reproductive age. It can cause irregular or absent periods, signs of too much male hormone (like excess hair growth, acne, or scalp hair loss), and sometimes small cysts on the ovaries. It can also make it harder to get pregnant and increases the risk of conditions like diabetes and heart disease. Every woman with PCOS is different — some have just one or two symptoms, others have many.

sections.heading: What causes it?
sections.content: The exact cause is not fully understood. PCOS involves a combination of genetic predisposition, insulin resistance (when the body doesn't use insulin efficiently), and hormonal imbalances. Environmental factors like diet and exercise levels also play a role. It tends to run in families — if your mother or sister has PCOS, you are more likely to have it too.

sections.heading: How is it diagnosed?
sections.content: There is no single test for PCOS. Your doctor will assess your symptoms, examine you, and carry out blood tests and possibly a pelvic ultrasound. The diagnosis is made using the Rotterdam Criteria — you need at least 2 of 3 features: irregular periods, signs of excess male hormones, or polycystic-looking ovaries on ultrasound. Other conditions causing similar symptoms must first be excluded with blood tests (thyroid, prolactin, certain adrenal hormones).

sections.heading: How is it treated?
sections.content: The foundation of PCOS treatment is lifestyle change — eating a healthy calorie-aware diet and exercising regularly. Even losing 5–10% of your body weight (if overweight) can significantly improve your symptoms and make it easier to conceive. If you don't want to become pregnant, the contraceptive pill is often recommended to regulate your periods and improve acne and excess hair. If you want to become pregnant, medications to stimulate ovulation (like letrozole) are very effective. Metformin (a diabetes medication) is often used to improve insulin resistance.

sections.heading: What about fertility?
sections.content: PCOS is the most common cause of irregular ovulation-related infertility, but most women with PCOS can have children. Treatments to trigger ovulation are very effective. Losing weight (if overweight) before starting fertility medications significantly improves the chances of success.

sections.heading: What are the long-term health risks?
sections.content: Women with PCOS have higher risks of: type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, heart disease, depression and anxiety, sleep apnoea (breathing problems during sleep), and endometrial (womb) cancer due to irregular periods. Regular health checks (blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol) are important. Your doctor will help you manage these risks.

sections.heading: Lifestyle tips
sections.content: Choose a balanced diet you can sustain — no single 'PCOS diet' works for everyone. Spread carbohydrates evenly across meals. Be physically active for at least 150 minutes per week. Avoid smoking. Manage stress, and seek help for low mood or anxiety. Remember — you don't need to lose a lot of weight to feel better; even a small amount of weight loss makes a real difference.

sections.heading: Where to get help
sections.content: Speak to your GP, gynaecologist, or endocrinologist. A registered dietitian can help with medical nutrition therapy. Mental health support is important if you are struggling with anxiety, depression, or body image. Patient support groups and reputable organisations (like Verity in the UK or PCOS Awareness Association) can also provide valuable support and information.

faq.question: What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?
faq.answer: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal disorder affecting women of reproductive age, characterized by a combination of hyperandrogenism (excess male hormones), ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. It is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age, affecting 8-13% of women worldwide. PCOS is a leading cause of anovulatory infertility and is associated with long-term metabolic complications including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and endometrial cancer.

faq.question: What causes PCOS?
faq.answer: The exact cause of PCOS is not fully understood, but it is multifactorial. Key contributing factors include: insulin resistance (present in 65-80% of women with PCOS), which drives excess androgen production from the ovaries; elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) levels stimulating androgen secretion; genetic predisposition (first-degree relatives have a 20-40% risk); low-grade chronic inflammation; and dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. Environmental factors such as obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and fetal programming (exposure to excess androgens in utero) also contribute.

faq.question: What are the symptoms of PCOS?
faq.answer: PCOS presents with a wide spectrum of symptoms, not all of which are present in every woman. Common symptoms include: irregular, infrequent, or absent menstrual periods (oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea); excessive hair growth on the face, chest, back, or abdomen (hirsutism); acne and oily skin; scalp hair thinning or male-pattern hair loss (androgenic alopecia); weight gain or difficulty losing weight, particularly around the abdomen; darkening of skin in body creases (acanthosis nigricans); skin tags; and difficulty getting pregnant due to irregular ovulation. Many women with PCOS also experience mood disorders including depression and anxiety.

faq.question: How is PCOS diagnosed?
faq.answer: PCOS is diagnosed using the Rotterdam Criteria (2003), which requires at least 2 of the following 3 features: (1) Oligo-ovulation or anovulation (irregular or absent periods); (2) Clinical or biochemical signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated serum androgens); (3) Polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (≥ 12 follicles measuring 2-9mm per ovary, or ovarian volume > 10 mL). Other conditions that mimic PCOS must be excluded, including thyroid disorders, hyperprolactinemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen-secreting tumors.

faq.question: What tests are done to diagnose PCOS?
faq.answer: Recommended investigations include: serum androgens (total and free testosterone, DHEAS, androstenedione); LH and FSH ratio (LH:FSH > 2:1 is supportive but not diagnostic); pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal preferred) to assess ovarian morphology; fasting glucose and insulin levels or oral glucose tolerance test (to assess insulin resistance); HbA1c; lipid profile; thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4); serum prolactin; and 17-hydroxyprogesterone (to exclude congenital adrenal hyperplasia). Pregnancy test should be done to rule out pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea.

faq.question: Who is most at risk for PCOS?
faq.answer: PCOS affects women of all ethnicities, but risk is higher in: women with a family history of PCOS (first-degree relatives have 20-40% lifetime risk); women with obesity or overweight (obesity worsens insulin resistance and androgen excess); daughters of mothers with PCOS or type 2 diabetes; women with early puberty or premature adrenarche; and women exposed to excess androgens in utero (e.g., daughters of women with PCOS). South Asian and Indigenous women may have higher prevalence and more severe metabolic manifestations.

faq.question: Does PCOS cause infertility?
faq.answer: PCOS is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility, accounting for approximately 80% of anovulatory infertility cases. Irregular or absent ovulation means eggs are not consistently released, making conception difficult. However, PCOS does not mean permanent infertility — most women with PCOS can conceive with treatment. Options include lifestyle modification (weight loss of 5-10% can restore ovulation in overweight women), ovulation induction with letrozole (first-line) or clomiphene citrate, metformin, gonadotropin injections, and assisted reproductive technologies (IVF) if other methods fail.

faq.question: What is the treatment for PCOS?
faq.answer: PCOS has no cure, but symptoms and risks can be effectively managed. Treatment is tailored to the individual's primary concerns: (1) Lifestyle modification — weight loss, regular exercise, and a balanced diet are first-line for all overweight women with PCOS, improving hormonal profiles, menstrual regularity, and fertility; (2) Menstrual regulation — combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are first-line for women not seeking pregnancy; (3) Hyperandrogenism — COCPs, spironolactone, or flutamide for hirsutism and acne; (4) Insulin resistance — metformin improves insulin sensitivity and menstrual regularity; (5) Fertility — letrozole (first-line ovulation inducer), clomiphene, gonadotropins, or IVF.

faq.question: What is the role of the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) in PCOS?
faq.answer: The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) is the first-line pharmacological treatment for managing menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in women with PCOS who do not want to conceive. COCPs suppress LH secretion (reducing ovarian androgen production), increase sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG, which binds free testosterone), and regulate menstrual cycles. They also reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer from chronic anovulation. Pills containing anti-androgenic progestogens (e.g., cyproterone acetate, drospirenone, desogestrel) are preferred for managing hirsutism and acne.

faq.question: What is the role of metformin in PCOS?
faq.answer: Metformin is an insulin-sensitizing agent used in PCOS to address the underlying insulin resistance. It reduces hepatic glucose production, improves peripheral insulin sensitivity, and lowers circulating insulin levels, which in turn reduces ovarian androgen production. Benefits include: improved menstrual regularity, modest reduction in androgen levels, weight stabilization, reduced risk of progression to type 2 diabetes, and improved ovulation rates (particularly when combined with letrozole for fertility). Metformin is recommended in women with PCOS who have impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes, or are at high metabolic risk.

faq.question: How does weight affect PCOS?
faq.answer: Obesity significantly worsens PCOS through amplified insulin resistance, which drives further androgen excess and anovulation. Even modest weight loss of 5-10% of body weight in overweight women with PCOS can significantly improve menstrual regularity, restore spontaneous ovulation, reduce androgen levels, improve acne and hirsutism, lower insulin and glucose levels, and improve fertility and response to ovulation induction. Weight loss is therefore the most effective intervention for overweight women with PCOS and is recommended before pharmacological treatment. However, PCOS itself makes weight loss more difficult due to insulin resistance and hormonal imbalances.

faq.question: What are the long-term health risks of PCOS?
faq.answer: PCOS is associated with significant long-term metabolic and reproductive health risks: type 2 diabetes (risk is 3-7 times higher than the general population; up to 40% of women with PCOS develop impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes by age 40); cardiovascular disease (dyslipidemia, hypertension, increased cardiovascular risk); endometrial cancer (2-6 times higher risk due to chronic unopposed estrogen from anovulation); obstructive sleep apnea (up to 30 times more common in PCOS); non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; and mental health disorders including depression, anxiety, and eating disorders. Regular screening for these conditions is recommended.

faq.question: What is the risk of endometrial cancer in PCOS?
faq.answer: Women with PCOS have a 2-6 times higher risk of endometrial cancer compared to the general population. This is caused by chronic anovulation, which results in prolonged exposure of the endometrium to estrogen without the opposing effect of progesterone (produced after ovulation). This leads to endometrial hyperplasia, which can progress to endometrial cancer if untreated. To reduce this risk, women with PCOS who are not ovulating regularly should have withdrawal bleeds induced at least every 3-4 months using progestogens or COCPs, and should be monitored with pelvic ultrasound if they have prolonged amenorrhea.

faq.question: Can PCOS be cured?
faq.answer: There is currently no cure for PCOS. It is a lifelong condition that persists beyond the reproductive years, though some symptoms (particularly menstrual irregularity) may improve with age or after menopause. However, the metabolic risks (type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease) persist after menopause. PCOS can be effectively managed with lifestyle changes and medications to control symptoms and reduce long-term health risks. Early diagnosis and proactive management are key to preventing complications.

faq.question: Does PCOS go away after menopause?
faq.answer: Some reproductive symptoms of PCOS, such as irregular periods, naturally resolve after menopause when the ovaries stop producing eggs. Androgen levels also decline after menopause. However, the underlying metabolic abnormalities — particularly insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and cardiovascular risk — persist and may worsen after menopause. Women with a history of PCOS remain at elevated risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome throughout their lives and should continue regular metabolic screening after menopause.

faq.question: What dietary and lifestyle changes help with PCOS?
faq.answer: Lifestyle modification is the cornerstone of PCOS management. Evidence-based recommendations include: a balanced, low-glycaemic index (low-GI) diet to reduce insulin spikes and improve insulin sensitivity; regular physical activity (at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week); weight loss of 5-10% in overweight women to restore hormonal balance and ovulation; reduced intake of refined carbohydrates, sugary foods, and processed foods; adequate sleep and stress management (chronic stress raises cortisol and worsens insulin resistance); and avoidance of smoking (which worsens hyperandrogenism and cardiovascular risk). Inositol supplements (myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol) show promising evidence for improving insulin sensitivity and ovarian function.

faq.question: What is the best contraceptive for women with PCOS?
faq.answer: The combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) is the preferred contraceptive for most women with PCOS as it simultaneously provides contraception, regulates menstrual cycles, reduces androgen levels, and protects the endometrium. Pills containing anti-androgenic progestogens (drospirenone, cyproterone acetate) are especially beneficial for women with hirsutism or acne. Progestogen-only pills or the hormonal IUD (levonorgestrel IUS) can be used to protect the endometrium in women who cannot take estrogen. The copper IUD is an effective non-hormonal option but does not address hormonal symptoms.

faq.question: Can PCOS affect mental health?
faq.answer: Yes. Women with PCOS have significantly higher rates of depression, anxiety, and reduced quality of life compared to the general population. Contributing factors include the psychological impact of symptoms such as hirsutism, acne, weight gain, hair loss, and infertility; hormonal imbalances (elevated androgens and insulin resistance affect brain neurotransmitter function); and the chronic nature of the condition. Screening for depression and anxiety is recommended as part of routine PCOS care. Treatment options include psychological support, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and medication where appropriate. Addressing the physical symptoms of PCOS also often improves mental wellbeing.

faq.question: Is PCOS hereditary?
faq.answer: Yes, PCOS has a strong genetic component. First-degree female relatives (mothers, sisters, daughters) of women with PCOS have a 20-40% lifetime risk of developing PCOS. Twin studies show concordance rates of up to 70% in identical twins. Several genes involved in insulin signaling, androgen biosynthesis, and gonadotropin regulation have been implicated. However, PCOS does not follow a simple inheritance pattern — it is polygenic and influenced by environmental factors including diet, weight, and physical activity. Sons of women with PCOS may carry related metabolic traits such as insulin resistance and elevated androgens.
